newsitem.title: YEMEN: High Yemen poll turnout overshadowed by violence.
newsitem.headline: High Yemen poll turnout overshadowed by violence.

text.p: Yemen reported a high voter turnout in the country's first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war, but two fatal shootings in which nine people died overshadowed Sunday's polling.
"There was a very big turnout of around 80 percent," Saeed-al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee, told a news conference in the capital Sanaa on Sunday night.

Before voting began, a soldier started shooting at people randomly at a polling station in the town of Mukayras, killing five soldiers and three civilians, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab said.
A Western election observer told Reuters a security official was shot dead in a separate incident on Sunday in the town of Dhamar, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Sanaa.
He said an armed Yemeni man had attempted to enter a polling station and began shooting when security personnel tried to disarm him. One official was injured and died after the attack.
The interior minister said the soldier who carried out the first shooting had been arrested and was being interrogated but there appeared to be no political motive for the killings.
But he added: "We were expecting more incidents because some people are discontented with holding general elections in Yemen." He did not elaborate.
Arab said one of the victims of the first attack was a member of Yemen's ruling party, the General Peoples Congress (GPC).
The election committee played down the violence, saying the attacks were "slight" and could have happened during elections anywhere in the world.

The incidents raised to four the number of election-related fatal attacks. A man was killed when clashes broke out between supporters of the GPC and its junior coalition partner, the Islamist Islah Party, in Ibb on April 20 and a child was killed in Taiz on Thursday when gunmen opened fire at a GPC rally.

The Republic of Yemen, formed in 1990 by the merger of conservative North Yemen and Marxist South Yemen, had not held parliamentary elections since a secessionist campaign by the south almost broke the country apart again in 1994.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war, and three others boycotted the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government denied their charges.

Diplomats predicted that President Ali Abdullah Saleh's GPC and Islah would retain power. Results were expected to start trickling in on Monday afternoon, but the final outcome was not likely to be known until later in the week.
A total of 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, stood for the 301 parliamentary seats, either under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.

Diplomats said the government hoped to boost its democratic image and provide the political stability needed to attract foreign investment and aid to the impoverished Arab state, a small oil producer.
They said they were encouraged by Yemen's democratic experiment but noted that power ultimately rested with the president, his appointed ministers and military and security forces loyal to the GPC.
